paragraphs: The Captain Cook Society places this statue in Hofgaard Park, a small triangular area in central Waimea between Kaumualii Highway and Waimea Road, almost outside the Bank of Hawaii building. The Hawaii State Foundation on Culture and the Arts bought the replica in 1978 from Derek & Patricia Freeborn, Ltd., for the 200th anniversary of Cook’s landing. It first stood at Waimea Canyon School and was later moved to the park.

The Garden Island reported in 2017 that the 15-foot figure faces the ocean and is a replica of the Whitby original. That account says Cook made first landfall at the mouth of the Waimea River in 1778. Plaques in the park carry a timeline of Waimea and Western influence. The plinth inscription recorded by the Captain Cook Society and Royal Museums Greenwich names Captain Cook, 1728–1779, and calls the work a replica of Sir John Tweed’s Whitby statue, placed through the State Foundation on Culture and the Arts and the Department of Accounting and General Services.

The same society page lists National Register and National Historic Landmark heritage notes and points readers to the Cook Landing Site. In September 2017 the county dedicated ADA walkways, ramps, benches, and an accessible picnic table in the one-third-acre park.

name: Captain James Cook Monument
title: Captain Cook Monument, Kealakekua Bay
description: A 27-foot concrete obelisk at Kaʻawaloa marks where Cook was killed in 1779. Reach the shore by trail or a permitted kayak tour.
subtitle: Kaʻawaloa, Kealakekua Bay
lede: The monument at Kaʻawaloa is a 27-foot concrete obelisk unveiled on November 14, 1874, near the place where Captain James Cook was killed on February 14, 1779.

facts.label: Builder
facts.value: Robert Lishman, for British Commissioner Wodehouse

facts.label: Entrance fee

paragraphs: Hawaii State Parks describes Kealakekua Bay State Historical Park as the site of the first extensive contact between Hawaiians and Westerners with Captain Cook’s arrival in 1779. The Captain Cook monument stands at Kaʻawaloa Flats, seen at a distance from the Nāpōʻopoʻo side. The park is open daily from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. with no entrance fee. Restrooms are only on the Nāpōʻopoʻo section.

A compilation of period newspapers on Images of Old Hawaiʻi says the present monument was unveiled on November 14, 1874. Robert Lishman built a plain obelisk on a square base, 27 feet high, of concrete made from screened pebbles and cement, on a leveled lava platform a few feet above the high-water mark. The Hawaiian Gazette account quoted there says the site was the gift of Princess Likelike. On January 26, 1877, Likelike and Archibald S. Cleghorn conveyed a 5,682-square-foot parcel for $1, in trust to British Commissioner James Hay Wodehouse, to keep a monument to Cook on the land. That page says the site is not simply owned by the British government and that tax records have listed the Captain Cook Monument Trust.

The Division of Aquatic Resources says Cook was killed in a skirmish on the shores of Kaʻawaloa Cove in February 1779 and that a 27-foot monument stands near that place. The bay is a Marine Life Conservation District of 315 acres, established in 1969. State Parks allows land access at Kaʻawaloa only by the Kaʻawaloa Trail or a guided kayak tour with a permitted vendor. Permitted vessels may transit the bay but may not land at Kaʻawaloa or launch from Nāpōʻopoʻo Wharf.

paragraphs: Lonely Planet says Charles Lindbergh, the first man to fly nonstop across the Atlantic, moved to remote Kīpahulu in 1968. After a terminal cancer diagnosis he stayed, died in 1974, and was buried in the graveyard of Palapala Hoʻomau Congregational Church. The grave is a simple granite slab laid on lava stones in the yard behind the church. The epitaph quotes the Bible: “If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea.”

SAH Archipedia dates the church to 1862, on the Hana Highway near mile marker 41, reached by a dirt drive at the first left after the marker when traveling south from Hana. It describes a plastered fieldstone church, renovated in 1965, with a stained-glass window of Jesus in a traditional Hawaiian feather cape. Lindbergh was interred in the cemetery in 1974. The iliʻili stones paving the grave are often taken and have to be replaced.

Mālama Hāna calls it a working church and private cemetery past ʻOheʻo, built in the mid-1800s of coral lime and lava rock, with the grave under java plum trees. There is no admission fee; donations are welcomed. There are no restrooms. Visitors are asked to stay quiet, stay on open paths, and not disturb services or graves.

paragraphs: The U.S. Pacific Fleet reported that a 9-foot bronze statue on a black granite pedestal was unveiled on September 2, 2013, at its permanent place next to the battleship USS Missouri on Ford Island. The ceremony marked the 68th anniversary of the signing of the Japanese surrender. The figure shows Nimitz as he appeared at the Battle of the Marshall Islands in 1944, when he commanded the largest ocean area and the most ships of any single commander. Sculptor Rip Caswell and his son unveiled it. The statue faces the USS Arizona Memorial.

The Naval Order of the United States, which commissioned the work, says the uniform is a wash-khaki short-sleeve shirt with rank insignia and a submarine-dolphin belt buckle, and that a horseshoe leans on the base because horseshoes were the admiral’s favorite pastime. The pedestal is absolute black granite. A gold-leaf quotation on the pedestal begins, “They fought together as brothers in arms.”

paragraphs: Go Hawaii says the bronze at International Market Place is positioned to welcome guests entering from Kalakaua Avenue. Oahu artist Kim Duffett depicted Ho in the 1970s. Ho was born Donald Tai Loy Ho in Kakaako on August 13, 1930, and died April 14, 2007. Duke Kahanamoku’s lounge at the original market place, known as Duke’s, is where he built the show that made him famous, including the hit “Tiny Bubbles.”

The Honolulu Star-Advertiser reported on July 16, 2017, that the statue would be unveiled on August 13 under the historic banyan at the Kalakaua entrance, a short distance from Duke’s, where Ho played from 1964 to 1970. Duffett said he wanted a 1970s performance pose, with a welcoming gesture. The widow, Haumea Hebenstreit Ho, said the statue stands 6 feet 4 inches and weighs between 400 and 500 pounds. Duffett’s own page lists the bronze as 76 by 26 by 20 inches, commissioned by Taubman Centers for International Market Place and completed in August 2017. paragraphs: Wikipedia describes Fagan’s Cross as a large stone cross on Lyon Hill in Hana, made of volcanic rock and completed in 1960, at 545 feet above sea level, at coordinates 20.7536 north, 155.9948 west. It memorializes San Francisco-born Paul Irving Fagan, Sr., who established cattle farming in Hana and built the town’s hotel in 1946. He was not buried at the cross. Wikipedia says he was interred at Cypress Lawn Memorial Park in California. The walk is a 1.5-mile round trip with about 500 feet of elevation gain, starting across from the Travaasa Hana hotel. Residents gather at the cross before sunrise on Easter for mass.

Hawaii Magazine’s 2019 guide says the lava-rock cross was erected in the early 1960s in memory of Paul Irving Fagan, Sr., who ran the 14,000-acre Hana Ranch and opened the Kauiki Inn in 1946, the hotel now called Travaasa Hana. The paved path crosses pasture owned by a land trust and climbs a little over 500 feet. The magazine says the land is private, livestock and cattle grates are on the path, and the trailhead landmark is the hotel at 5031 Hana Highway. A small wooden gate to the left of the parking lot begins the walk. From the hill you can see Hana Bay and the east Maui coast.

paragraphs: Wikipedia places Kalākaua Park at 19.72528 north, 155.08861 west, in the block bounded by Waianuenue Avenue, Kalākaua Avenue, Kinoole Street, and Keawe Street. The park was completed in February 1934 on the old courthouse site. The bronze of King Kalākaua, sculpted and cast by Henry Bianchini, was dedicated on August 6, 1988, with a time capsule in its base. A second capsule was buried in 1991 during a total solar eclipse. Bianchini chose a seated pose so the king would be closer to people and would not be lost in the banyan branches. The figure holds a taro leaf, for the bond with the land, and an ipu, for the revival of chant and hula. Donations totaling $40,000 paid for the statue. Kalākaua ruled from 1874 to 1891 and is called the Merrie Monarch. The festival of that name is held annually in Hilo.

Kaʻahele Hawaiʻi also describes Bianchini’s bronze in the middle of the park, holding a taro leaf and an ipu heke, and notes the 1991 eclipse capsule. The park still has the sundial from the king’s era, a reflecting pond, and the marble war memorial to Hawaii Island dead of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam.

paragraphs: Hank Soboleski, writing in The Garden Island on April 29, 2018, said dedication services on the afternoon of Sunday, April 20, 1930, were chaired by K. Miyasaki and S. Takata. Japanese residents of Kealia had just erected the monument for former Makee Sugar Company owner Colonel Zephaniah S. Spalding (1837–1927). At the dedication, Philip L. Rice said Captain James Makee founded Makee Sugar Company in 1877 and that after Makee’s death in 1878 Spalding bought a majority interest. Images of Old Hawaiʻi adds that the monument sits on a high point of the old Makee plantation lands and that Spalding was born September 2, 1837, in Warren, Ohio, and died in Pasadena on June 19, 1927.

paragraphs: Common Ground Kauai says the Stone Dam was built in the late 1800s by the Kilauea Sugar Plantation. Each stone was carved and placed to raise the water level 20 feet and feed a gravity irrigation system for the cane fields. Angled buttresses were meant to carry the water’s weight and to let ʻoʻopu, the Hawaiian freshwater goby, move upstream. Hawaii Land Trust lists the Kilauea stone dam, built in the 1880s, among the features of the Wai Koa Loop Trail protected in 2019 by a conservation easement.

The same Common Ground page says the dam is part of the public 4.5-mile Wai Koa Loop, normally reached through the North Shore Dog Park on Kahiliholo Road, dawn to dusk, with a waiver at the trailhead. It also says that because of Hurricane Lowell the trail to the Stone Dam is closed until further notice. Anaina Hou, which has another entrance, likewise reports hurricane damage at its trailhead. There are no restrooms or drinking water on the trail.

paragraphs: The Honolulu Advertiser on March 8, 2007, said Hawaii Volcanoes National Park had unveiled “Ulumau Pohaku Pele” the day before. title: Alburnett Moai, Linn County
description: Steve Piper’s 14-foot steel moai stands in a field on George Etzel’s Alburnett farm. It was set on a concrete pad in spring 2009.
subtitle: A private moai near Alburnett, Iowa
lede: Cedar Rapids sculptor Steve Piper built a 14-foot steel moai for George Etzel’s farm near Alburnett. A crane set it on a concrete pad in the spring of 2009.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Steel plate on a rod frame, about 3,000 pounds

paragraphs: The Gazette’s August 5, 2009, column says George Etzel had a 14-foot Easter Island head made for his Alburnett farm in Linn County. Sculptor Steve Piper of Cedar Rapids spent about a year and a half on a 14-foot-tall, 8-foot-wide, 3,000-pound steel moai. It was built to rust, and Piper sprayed it with salt water to help the patina. A crane set it that spring on a concrete platform. The column says the platform was about 400 feet from the house and that a gravel road passes to the east. Etzel said cars stop and people get out to photograph it. Some walk closer and discover the “wood” is metal.

The Gazette’s companion story the day before says the moai stands in a 12-acre field north of the house, weighs between 2,500 and 3,000 pounds, and was placed about 400 yards from the house. Both stories agree on the maker, the 14-foot height, the steel construction, the half-inch rod frame, 12-gauge plates, and 11 yards of concrete. Piper studied architecture at Iowa State and worked at the Cedar Rapids Assessor’s Office. The farm is private. The opened pages do not give a street address.

see_items.title: The head
see_items.text: A 14-foot moai, 8 feet wide in the August 5 account, built of rusted steel.

see_items.title: The frame
see_items.text: Half-inch steel rods under 12-gauge plates, on a thick steel base.

see_items.title: The road
see_items.text: A gravel road runs east of the field. Drivers stop to look.

tips: This is a private farm. The Gazette describes people photographing from the roadside, not a staffed attraction.
Do not climb the sculpture. The stories do not invite visitors into the field.
No street address was published in the pages opened. Do not treat a guessed rural range as the location.
The two Gazette columns disagree on whether the figure is about 400 feet or about 400 yards from the house, so that distance is left unstated as a single fact.

faq.a: Steve Piper of Cedar Rapids, for George Etzel.
The August 5, 2009, Gazette column says 14 feet tall, 8 feet wide, and about 3,000 pounds.
Steel. A rod frame is covered with 12-gauge plate, and the piece was encouraged to rust.
In the spring of 2009, by crane, on a concrete pad. The Gazette columns ran in August 2009.
It is on a private Alburnett farm. The paper says cars on the gravel road stop for photographs. It does not list public hours or an address.

sources: Sources: The Gazette, “Magnificent Moai,” Aug. 5, 2009; The Gazette, “Easter Island replicas starts man’s outdoor art collection,” Aug. 4, 2009. Last checked October 21, 2026.
removed_claims: A width of 9 feet was not used. The August 5 column says 8 feet.
A claim that the steel was made to look like concrete was not supported. Viewers in the story mistook it for wood.
The address range 3999–4199 E Otter Road was not on the pages opened.
The two columns disagree on 400 feet versus 400 yards from the house.
